COMPENSATORY EQUITY PLAN SECURITIES EXEMPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, states what California and federal law provide about the securities-law exemption a corporation or limited liability company commonly relies on when it issues stock options, restricted stock, or other equity awards to its own workforce under a written equity plan — here, Acme, Inc.'s plan identified as: 2026 Equity Incentive Plan. That exemption, California Corporations Code § 25102(o), is a different provision from this project's existing California Limited Offering Exemption information sheet, which addresses Corporations Code § 25102(f) — a private-placement exemption capped at 35 purchasers and conditioned on a preexisting relationship or investor sophistication — and from this project's existing California Notice Filing for Federally Covered Rule 506 Offerings clause, which addresses Corporations Code § 25102.1's separate notice-filing regime for offerings that raise outside investment capital under federal Regulation D. Section 25102(o) instead exempts compensatory equity issued to an issuer's own employees, directors, and certain other service providers under a written plan, by incorporating a federal exemption — Rule 701 of the Securities Act of 1933 (17 C.F.R. § 230.701) — and adding California-specific conditions of its own. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any specific plan, grant, or issuance by Acme, Inc. meets the conditions of this exemption, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

CALIFORNIA'S COMPENSATORY BENEFIT PLAN EXEMPTION FROM SECURITIES QUALIFICATION
California Corporations Code § 25102(o) exempts from the state's securities qualification requirement (Corporations Code § 25110) an offer or sale of a security issued by a corporation or limited liability company under a purchase plan or agreement, or under an option plan or agreement, provided the security is exempt from federal registration under Rule 701 at the time of issuance or grant. The statute does not create a freestanding state-law standard; it incorporates Rule 701's federal conditions by reference and then layers on three further, California-specific conditions: a purchase plan or agreement must comply with 10 California Code of Regulations §§ 260.140.42, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46; an option plan or agreement must comply with 10 California Code of Regulations §§ 260.140.41, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46; and the issuer must file a notice of transaction with the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation no later than 30 days after the initial issuance of any security under the plan, accompanied by a filing fee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(o) An offer or sale of any security issued by a corporation or limited liability company pursuant to a purchase plan or agreement, or issued pursuant to an option plan or agreement, where the security at the time of issuance or grant is exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, pursuant to Rule 701 adopted pursuant to that act (17 C.F.R. 230.701), the provisions of which are hereby incorporated by reference into this section, provided that (1) the terms of any purchase plan or agreement shall comply with Sections 260.140.42, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46 of Title 10 of the California Code of Regulations, (2) the terms of any option plan or agreement shall comply with Sections 260.140.41, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46 of Title 10 of the California Code of Regulations, and (3) the issuer files a notice of transaction in accordance with rules adopted by the commissioner no later than 30 days after the initial issuance of any security under that plan, accompanied by a filing fee as prescribed by subdivision (y) of Section 25608."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o), California Corporations Code, the compensatory benefit plan exemption from securities qualification, incorporating Rule 701 and layering on state regulatory and notice-filing conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)

Code § 25102(o) itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical (the raw HTML places a non-breaking space, not a plain space, immediately after the “(o)” subsection label — verified in the raw HTML and normalized to a plain space in the quote below). Of the four California Code of Regulations sections this subdivision cross-references, this document independently fetched and separately quotes only two — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.41 (compensatory option plans) and 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.46 (financial statements to security holders), both from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror — in later clauses of this same document; 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.42 (compensatory purchase plans) and § 260.140.45 were not independently fetched or verified this session, so this clause does not state their substantive content, only that § 25102(o) requires compliance with them. The filing fee amount under Corporations Code § 25608(y), referenced by § 25102(o) itself, was likewise not independently fetched. This clause does not determine whether any specific plan, grant, or issuance by a given company in fact meets Rule 701's conditions or these California regulatory conditions.

THE NOTICE FILING'S CURE PROVISION AND THE SINGLE-OFFERING RULE
The same subdivision that imposes the 30-day notice-filing requirement also provides two further rules. First, missing the 30-day deadline does not, by the statute's own text, cause the exemption to be lost: an issuer that fails to timely file must instead file the notice and pay an additional, larger fee — equal to what the full qualification fee under Section 25110 would have been — within 15 business days after discovering the failure or after the Commissioner demands it, whichever comes first. Second, all offers and sales made in reliance on this exemption are treated as a single, discrete offering that is not integrated with any other offering or sale by the issuer, whether that other offering is qualified under the general qualification statute, separately exempt, or not subject to qualification at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The failure to file the notice of transaction within the time specified in this subdivision shall not affect the availability of this exemption. An issuer that fails to file the notice shall, within 15 business days after discovery of the failure to file the notice or after demand by the commissioner, whichever occurs first, file the notice and pay the commissioner a fee equal to the maximum aggregate fee payable had the transaction been qualified under Section 25110."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o), California Corporations Code, the cure provision for a late or missed notice of transaction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  "Offers and sales exempt pursuant to this subdivision shall be deemed to be part of a single, discrete offering and are not subject to integration with any other offering or sale, whether qualified under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 25110), or otherwise exempt, or not subject to qualification."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o), California Corporations Code, the single-discrete-offering / no-integration rule for offers and sales exempt under this subdivision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  Known gap: Both quotations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o), immediately following the sentence quoted in the preceding clause of this document — they are not independent sources of each other or of that clause. Fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical. The raw HTML places the first quoted sentence and the second in separate, adjacent paragraph elements with no whitespace character between them at all (the source text reads “...qualified under Section 25110.Offers and sales...” with no space before “Offers”) — verified in the raw HTML; this clause quotes the two sentences as two separate citation entries rather than bridging that gap with an invented space. This clause does not address what “filing the notice” and “paying the fee” after a missed deadline require procedurally, and does not state the dollar amount of either fee.

RULE 701'S FEDERAL EXEMPTION, ITS COEXISTENCE WITH STATE LAW, AND WHICH ISSUERS MAY USE IT
Rule 701, adopted by the Securities and Exchange Commission under the Securities Act of 1933, exempts from federal registration an offer or sale of securities made in compliance with all of the rule's conditions. The rule's own preliminary notes state that satisfying it does not excuse compliance with any other body of law: an issuer relying on Rule 701 must still comply with any applicable state securities law — which, for a California issuer or an offering reaching California persons, is where Corporations Code § 25102(o)'s own additional conditions come in. Rule 701 is also not available to every issuer: by its own terms, it is available only to an issuer that is not subject to the reporting requirements of Exchange Act § 13 or § 15(d) (that is, a company that does not already file periodic reports with the SEC) and that is not an investment company registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Exemption. Offers and sales made in compliance with all of the conditions of this section are exempt from section 5 of the Act (15 U.S.C. 77e)."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(a), Securities Act Rule 701, the federal exemption from registration (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  "2. In addition to complying with this section, the issuer also must comply with any applicable state law relating to the offer and sale of securities."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701, Preliminary Note 2, Securities Act Rule 701, preliminary note that compliance with the rule does not excuse compliance with applicable state securities law (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  "(1) General. This section is available to any issuer that is not subject to the reporting requirements of section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Exchange Act”) (15 U.S.C. 78m or 78o(d)) and is not an investment company registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-1 et seq.)."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(b)(1), Securities Act Rule 701, general issuer-eligibility condition (non-reporting company, not a registered investment company) (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  Known gap: The first and third quotations below come from 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(a) and § 230.701(b)(1) respectively — numbered, operative subsections of the rule; the second quotation comes from the rule's unnumbered “Preliminary Notes,” which the eCFR's rendering of the rule presents as introductory text preceding subsection (a) rather than as a lettered subsection in its own right, and which this clause treats as guidance on the rule's scope rather than as an independently operative conditional requirement. All three were fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov, using two different User-Agent headers (a realistic browser string, since eCFR redirects non-browser User-Agents), and found byte-identical apart from an expected per-request script nonce value in the page's analytics tag. This clause does not address Rule 701(b)(2) or (b)(3), which extend the exemption to certain issuers that later become reporting companies or that merely guarantee a subsidiary's securities — narrower situations not addressed here.

WHO MAY RECEIVE SECURITIES UNDER THE EXEMPTION
Rule 701 exempts offers and sales made under a written compensatory benefit plan or written compensation contract established by the issuer (or its parent or majority-owned subsidiaries) for the participation of a defined group: employees, directors, general partners, trustees of a business-trust issuer, officers, and consultants and advisors, together with family members who acquire the securities from one of those persons by gift or under a domestic relations order. A former member of one of these groups may still receive an exempt offer, but only if the person was employed by, or providing services to, the issuer at the time the securities were offered — an offer made after the relationship has already ended falls outside this exemption on the rule's own terms. The rule also expands "employee" to include certain exclusive insurance agents of the issuer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) Transactions exempted by this section. This section exempts offers and sales of securities (including plan interests and guarantees pursuant to paragraph (d)(2)(ii) of this section) under a written compensatory benefit plan (or written compensation contract) established by the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent, for the participation of their employees, directors, general partners, trustees (where the issuer is a business trust), officers, or consultants and advisors, and their family members who acquire such securities from such persons through gifts or domestic relations orders. This section exempts offers and sales to former employees, directors, general partners, trustees, officers, consultants and advisors only if such persons were employed by or providing services to the issuer at the time the securities were offered. In addition, the term “employee” includes insurance agents who are exclusive agents of the issuer, its subsidiaries or parents, or derive more than 50% of their annual income from those entities."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c), Securities Act Rule 701, the defined group of eligible recipients and the former-service-provider condition (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  Known gap: This clause quotes 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause states the general eligible-recipient group and the former-service-provider limitation; it does not address the rule's separate treatment of guarantees under paragraph (d)(2)(ii) mentioned in this same subsection's opening clause, which this clause does not independently trace or explain. This is federal law that applies the same way regardless of which state's law otherwise governs a specific plan; it does not by itself address who may receive securities under California's own, separately conditioned exemption.

CONSULTANTS AND ADVISORS' SPECIAL CONDITIONS, AND WHAT COUNTS AS A "COMPENSATORY BENEFIT PLAN"
Not every consultant or advisor to an issuer qualifies for this exemption. Rule 701 makes it available to a consultant or advisor only if the person is a natural person (not an entity), provides bona fide services to the issuer or a qualifying parent or subsidiary, and the services are not connected to a capital-raising securities offer or sale and do not promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities — a condition aimed at keeping this exemption for genuine service providers rather than for a substitute channel to raise investment capital or create trading liquidity. Separately, the rule defines what plans this exemption reaches: a "compensatory benefit plan" is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension, or similar plan.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) Special requirements for consultants and advisors. This section is available to consultants and advisors only if: (i) They are natural persons; (ii) They provide bona fide services to the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent; and (iii) The services are not in connection with the offer or sale of securities in a capital-raising transaction, and do not directly or indirectly promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c)(1), Securities Act Rule 701, special conditions limiting the exemption for consultants and advisors (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  "(2) Definition of “compensatory benefit plan.” For purposes of this section, a compensatory benefit plan is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension or similar plan."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c)(2), Securities Act Rule 701, definition of "compensatory benefit plan" (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two subparagraphs of the same rule, 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c)(1) and (c)(2), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not address subparagraph (c)(3), the rule's separate definition of "family member," which lists specific relationships and is not restated here. This clause does not determine whether any specific person's relationship to a given issuer in fact qualifies as bona fide consulting or advisory services under this condition.

THE ROLLING 12-MONTH DOLLAR AND PERCENTAGE CEILING ON SALES
Rule 701 does not cap the amount of securities an issuer may offer, but it does cap the aggregate sales price or amount of securities actually sold in reliance on the exemption during any rolling 12-month period. That ceiling is the greatest of three alternative measures: $1,000,000; 15% of the issuer's total assets (measured at its most recent balance sheet date, if no older than its last fiscal year end); or 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on the exemption, measured the same way. Because the statute takes the greatest of these three figures, a larger or asset-heavy issuer's usable ceiling under this exemption can substantially exceed the flat $1,000,000 figure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(2) Sales. The aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold in reliance on this section during any consecutive 12-month period must not exceed the greatest of the following: (i) $1,000,000; (ii) 15% of the total assets of the issuer (or of the issuer's parent if the issuer is a wholly-owned subsidiary and the securities represent obligations that the parent fully and unconditionally guarantees), measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end); or (iii) 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on this section, measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end)."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(d)(2), Securities Act Rule 701, the 12-month aggregate sales ceiling and its three alternative measures (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  Known gap: This clause quotes 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(d)(2), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not restate paragraph (d)(1) (the separate, uncapped rule for mere offers, as distinct from completed sales) or paragraph (d)(3)'s detailed rules for calculating "aggregate sales price" and the timing of that calculation for options and deferred-compensation plans — both addressed by the same subsection but not quoted here. This clause does not calculate, and does not state, what a specific issuer's own applicable ceiling is under any of the three alternative measures.

THE $10 MILLION DISCLOSURE TRIGGER
Below a certain scale, Rule 701 requires only that the issuer deliver a copy of the compensatory benefit plan or contract itself. But once the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold under the exemption during any rolling 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the rule requires the issuer to deliver additional disclosure to investors a reasonable time before the date of sale — including a summary of the plan's material terms (or, for an ERISA-covered plan, the ERISA summary plan description), risk-factor information about the securities, and specified financial statements. This $10 million figure is measured the same way, and over the same rolling 12-month window, as the aggregate sales ceiling addressed elsewhere in this document — it is a disclosure trigger layered on top of that ceiling, not a separate transaction limit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In addition, if the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold during any consecutive 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the issuer must deliver the following disclosure to investors a reasonable period of time before the date of sale:"
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(e), Securities Act Rule 701, the $10 million rolling 12-month disclosure trigger (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-230/subject-group-ECFR6b9820af1bfaf3d/section-230.701)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the introductory sentence of 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(e), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not restate the five enumerated disclosure items themselves (paragraphs (e)(1) through (e)(5)) in the level of specific, item-by-item detail the rule sets out — including the specific financial-statement staleness limit of 180 days before sale, and the special timing rules for options and deferred-compensation elections — nor does it address paragraph (e)(6)'s separate timing rule for stock options and deferred compensation. This clause does not determine whether any specific issuer's own sales under any specific plan have crossed, or are projected to cross, this $10 million threshold.

CALIFORNIA'S REQUIRED TERMS FOR A COMPENSATORY OPTION PLAN
Where an issuer's plan grants options rather than selling shares outright, California's implementing regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.41, requires the option plan or agreement itself to contain specific protective terms in order for the underlying grants to qualify for this state exemption. Two of those required terms set outer limits on how the option may be structured: the option's exercise period may not exceed 120 months from the date it is granted, and — unless the option holder's employment is terminated for cause — the right to exercise an already-vested option must remain open for at least 6 months after termination caused by death or disability, or at least 30 days after a termination for any other reason, in each case until no later than the option's own expiration date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) An exercise period of not more than 120 months from the date the option is granted."
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.41(b), California Code of Regulations, the 120-month maximum exercise period for a compensatory option (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.140.41)
  "(e) Unless employment is terminated for cause as defined by applicable law, the terms of the plan or option grant or a contract of employment, the right to exercise in the event of termination of employment, to the extent that the optionee is entitled to exercise on the date employment terminates, continues until the earlier of the option expiration date or: (1) At least 6 months from the date of termination if termination was caused by death or disability. (2) At least 30 days from the date of termination if termination was caused by other than death or disability."
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.41(e), California Code of Regulations, the minimum post-termination exercise window for a vested compensatory option (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.140.41)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two lettered subsections of the same regulation, 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.41(b) and (e), fetched twice this session from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror (law.cornell.edu) using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization. As in the corpus's existing California Limited Offering Exemption document, this regulation's text was verified only against the Cornell mirror; the official state platform (govt.westlaw.com, operated under contract with the Office of Administrative Law) could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch during this research, so this citation was not independently cross-checked against that primary state-hosted source. This clause does not restate the regulation's remaining required terms — the total-number-of-securities and eligible-persons disclosure of subsection (a), the non-transferability condition of subsection (c), the anti-dilution adjustment of subsection (d), the 10-year outer limit on granting options under the plan in subsection (f), the security-holder-approval condition of subsection (g) (with its narrow foreign-private-issuer carve-out), or the cross-reference to the financial-statement regulation in subsection (h), addressed separately elsewhere in this document — none of which are quoted here. This is a California-specific regulatory condition layered on top of, not a restatement of, Rule 701's own federal conditions addressed elsewhere in this document.

THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT REQUIREMENT TO SECURITY HOLDERS
A separate California regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.46, requires that a plan or agreement under which securities are issued to employees, officers, directors, managers, advisors, or consultants — including option, purchase, and bonus plans — provide that the security holder will receive financial statements at least annually. This requirement does not mandate any particular accounting standard for those statements. It also does not apply in two situations: where issuance is limited to key persons whose role with the issuer already gives them access to equivalent information, and where the plan or agreement complies with all of Rule 701's own conditions — in which case, for purposes of judging that Rule 701 compliance, the regulation treats a registered domestic partner as a "family member" within Rule 701's own definition of that term.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Plans or agreements pursuant to which securities are to be issued to employees, officers, directors, managers, advisors or consultants (including option, purchase and bonus plans) shall provide that the security holder(s) will receive financial statements at least annually. This section does not require the use of financial statements in accordance with Section 260.613 of these rules. This section shall not apply when issuance is limited to key persons whose duties in connection with the issuer assure them access to equivalent information. This section shall not apply to any plan or agreement that complies with all conditions of Rule 701 of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (17 C.F.R. 230.701); provided that for purposes of determining such compliance, any registered domestic partner shall be considered a "family member" as that term is defined in Rule 701."
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.46, California Code of Regulations, the annual financial statement requirement and its key-person and Rule 701 carve-outs (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.140.46)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the operative paragraph of 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.46, fetched twice this session from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror (law.cornell.edu) using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization; as with the preceding clause, this regulation was not independently cross-checked against the state's own Westlaw-hosted platform, which could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch this session. This clause does not independently verify 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.613, cross-referenced here only to say that this regulation does not require financial statements prepared in accordance with it. This clause does not determine whether any specific recipient under a given plan qualifies as a "key person" for purposes of the first carve-out, or whether a given issuer's plan in fact complies with all of Rule 701's conditions for purposes of the second.

STATEMENT IDENTIFYING THE PLAN DESCRIBED
This information sheet is prepared in connection with Acme, Inc.'s plan identified as: 2026 Equity Incentive Plan, under which the type of award(s) described is: incentive stock options. Recording this identifying information here does not determine that Acme, Inc., this plan, or any specific grant or issuance under it in fact satisfies Rule 701, Corporations Code § 25102(o), or any California Code of Regulations section addressed in this document.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan Lee, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of Rule 701 (17 C.F.R. § 230.701), California Corporations Code § 25102(o), and the California Code of Regulations sections addressed in this document, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not evaluate whether any offer, sale, or grant of a security by Acme, Inc. under 2026 Equity Incentive Plan meets the conditions of these exemptions, whether any required California notice of transaction was properly or timely filed, or whether any other exemption (federal or state) is available or was properly relied upon, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

expectedJSON.body: The same subdivision that imposes the 30-day notice-filing requirement also provides two further rules. First, missing the 30-day deadline does not, by the statute's own text, cause the exemption to be lost: an issuer that fails to timely file must instead file the notice and pay an additional, larger fee — equal to what the full qualification fee under Section 25110 would have been — within 15 business days after discovering the failure or after the Commissioner demands it, whichever comes first. Second, all offers and sales made in reliance on this exemption are treated as a single, discrete offering that is not integrated with any other offering or sale by the issuer, whether that other offering is qualified under the general qualification statute, separately exempt, or not subject to qualification at all.

citations.quote: The failure to file the notice of transaction within the time specified in this subdivision shall not affect the availability of this exemption. An issuer that fails to file the notice shall, within 15 business days after discovery of the failure to file the notice or after demand by the commissioner, whichever occurs first, file the notice and pay the commissioner a fee equal to the maximum aggregate fee payable had the transaction been qualified under Section 25110.

citations.quote: Offers and sales exempt pursuant to this subdivision shall be deemed to be part of a single, discrete offering and are not subject to integration with any other offering or sale, whether qualified under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 25110), or otherwise exempt, or not subject to qualification.

expectedJSON.body: Rule 701, adopted by the Securities and Exchange Commission under the Securities Act of 1933, exempts from federal registration an offer or sale of securities made in compliance with all of the rule's conditions. The rule's own preliminary notes state that satisfying it does not excuse compliance with any other body of law: an issuer relying on Rule 701 must still comply with any applicable state securities law — which, for a California issuer or an offering reaching California persons, is where Corporations Code § 25102(o)'s own additional conditions come in. Rule 701 is also not available to every issuer: by its own terms, it is available only to an issuer that is not subject to the reporting requirements of Exchange Act § 13 or § 15(d) (that is, a company that does not already file periodic reports with the SEC) and that is not an investment company registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, the federal exemption from registration
citations.quote: (a) Exemption. Offers and sales made in compliance with all of the conditions of this section are exempt from section 5 of the Act (15 U.S.C. 77e).

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, preliminary note that compliance with the rule does not excuse compliance with applicable state securities law
citations.quote: 2. In addition to complying with this section, the issuer also must comply with any applicable state law relating to the offer and sale of securities.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, general issuer-eligibility condition (non-reporting company, not a registered investment company)
citations.quote: (1) General. This section is available to any issuer that is not subject to the reporting requirements of section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Exchange Act”) (15 U.S.C. 78m or 78o(d)) and is not an investment company registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-1 et seq.).

expectedJSON.body: Rule 701 exempts offers and sales made under a written compensatory benefit plan or written compensation contract established by the issuer (or its parent or majority-owned subsidiaries) for the participation of a defined group: employees, directors, general partners, trustees of a business-trust issuer, officers, and consultants and advisors, together with family members who acquire the securities from one of those persons by gift or under a domestic relations order. A former member of one of these groups may still receive an exempt offer, but only if the person was employed by, or providing services to, the issuer at the time the securities were offered — an offer made after the relationship has already ended falls outside this exemption on the rule's own terms. The rule also expands "employee" to include certain exclusive insurance agents of the issuer.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, the defined group of eligible recipients and the former-service-provider condition
citations.quote: (c) Transactions exempted by this section. This section exempts offers and sales of securities (including plan interests and guarantees pursuant to paragraph (d)(2)(ii) of this section) under a written compensatory benefit plan (or written compensation contract) established by the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent, for the participation of their employees, directors, general partners, trustees (where the issuer is a business trust), officers, or consultants and advisors, and their family members who acquire such securities from such persons through gifts or domestic relations orders. This section exempts offers and sales to former employees, directors, general partners, trustees, officers, consultants and advisors only if such persons were employed by or providing services to the issuer at the time the securities were offered. In addition, the term “employee” includes insurance agents who are exclusive agents of the issuer, its subsidiaries or parents, or derive more than 50% of their annual income from those entities.

expectedJSON.body: Not every consultant or advisor to an issuer qualifies for this exemption. Rule 701 makes it available to a consultant or advisor only if the person is a natural person (not an entity), provides bona fide services to the issuer or a qualifying parent or subsidiary, and the services are not connected to a capital-raising securities offer or sale and do not promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities — a condition aimed at keeping this exemption for genuine service providers rather than for a substitute channel to raise investment capital or create trading liquidity. Separately, the rule defines what plans this exemption reaches: a "compensatory benefit plan" is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension, or similar plan.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, special conditions limiting the exemption for consultants and advisors
citations.quote: (1) Special requirements for consultants and advisors. This section is available to consultants and advisors only if: (i) They are natural persons; (ii) They provide bona fide services to the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent; and (iii) The services are not in connection with the offer or sale of securities in a capital-raising transaction, and do not directly or indirectly promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, definition of "compensatory benefit plan"
citations.quote: (2) Definition of “compensatory benefit plan.” For purposes of this section, a compensatory benefit plan is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension or similar plan.

This clause does not determine whether any specific person's relationship to a given issuer in fact qualifies as bona fide consulting or advisory services under this condition.

expectedJSON.body: Rule 701 does not cap the amount of securities an issuer may offer, but it does cap the aggregate sales price or amount of securities actually sold in reliance on the exemption during any rolling 12-month period. That ceiling is the greatest of three alternative measures: $1,000,000; 15% of the issuer's total assets (measured at its most recent balance sheet date, if no older than its last fiscal year end); or 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on the exemption, measured the same way. Because the statute takes the greatest of these three figures, a larger or asset-heavy issuer's usable ceiling under this exemption can substantially exceed the flat $1,000,000 figure.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, the 12-month aggregate sales ceiling and its three alternative measures
citations.quote: (2) Sales. The aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold in reliance on this section during any consecutive 12-month period must not exceed the greatest of the following: (i) $1,000,000; (ii) 15% of the total assets of the issuer (or of the issuer's parent if the issuer is a wholly-owned subsidiary and the securities represent obligations that the parent fully and unconditionally guarantees), measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end); or (iii) 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on this section, measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end).

expectedJSON.body: Below a certain scale, Rule 701 requires only that the issuer deliver a copy of the compensatory benefit plan or contract itself. But once the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold under the exemption during any rolling 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the rule requires the issuer to deliver additional disclosure to investors a reasonable time before the date of sale — including a summary of the plan's material terms (or, for an ERISA-covered plan, the ERISA summary plan description), risk-factor information about the securities, and specified financial statements. This $10 million figure is measured the same way, and over the same rolling 12-month window, as the aggregate sales ceiling addressed elsewhere in this document — it is a disclosure trigger layered on top of that ceiling, not a separate transaction limit.

citations.quote: In addition, if the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold during any consecutive 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the issuer must deliver the following disclosure to investors a reasonable period of time before the date of sale:

expectedJSON.body: Where an issuer's plan grants options rather than selling shares outright, California's implementing regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.41, requires the option plan or agreement itself to contain specific protective terms in order for the underlying grants to qualify for this state exemption. Two of those required terms set outer limits on how the option may be structured: the option's exercise period may not exceed 120 months from the date it is granted, and — unless the option holder's employment is terminated for cause — the right to exercise an already-vested option must remain open for at least 6 months after termination caused by death or disability, or at least 30 days after a termination for any other reason, in each case until no later than the option's own expiration date.

citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, the 120-month maximum exercise period for a compensatory option
citations.quote: (b) An exercise period of not more than 120 months from the date the option is granted.

citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, the minimum post-termination exercise window for a vested compensatory option
citations.quote: (e) Unless employment is terminated for cause as defined by applicable law, the terms of the plan or option grant or a contract of employment, the right to exercise in the event of termination of employment, to the extent that the optionee is entitled to exercise on the date employment terminates, continues until the earlier of the option expiration date or: (1) At least 6 months from the date of termination if termination was caused by death or disability. (2) At least 30 days from the date of termination if termination was caused by other than death or disability.

expectedJSON.body: A separate California regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.46, requires that a plan or agreement under which securities are issued to employees, officers, directors, managers, advisors, or consultants — including option, purchase, and bonus plans — provide that the security holder will receive financial statements at least annually. This requirement does not mandate any particular accounting standard for those statements. It also does not apply in two situations: where issuance is limited to key persons whose role with the issuer already gives them access to equivalent information, and where the plan or agreement complies with all of Rule 701's own conditions — in which case, for purposes of judging that Rule 701 compliance, the regulation treats a registered domestic partner as a "family member" within Rule 701's own definition of that term.

citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, the annual financial statement requirement and its key-person and Rule 701 carve-outs
citations.quote: Plans or agreements pursuant to which securities are to be issued to employees, officers, directors, managers, advisors or consultants (including option, purchase and bonus plans) shall provide that the security holder(s) will receive financial statements at least annually. This section does not require the use of financial statements in accordance with Section 260.613 of these rules. This section shall not apply when issuance is limited to key persons whose duties in connection with the issuer assure them access to equivalent information. This section shall not apply to any plan or agreement that complies with all conditions of Rule 701 of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (17 C.F.R. 230.701); provided that for purposes of determining such compliance, any registered domestic partner shall be considered a "family member" as that term is defined in Rule 701.
